messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 53
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Tax Consultant
- Trauma Type: Police violence
- Pcl5: 57

He is 53, a Latin American man who has spent most of his adult life working carefully and quietly as a tax consultant. He describes himself as someone who has always trusted numbers more than people. Before everything happened, his days had a dependable rhythm: early coffee, pressed shirts, client calls, long hours reviewing returns and explaining rules that most people find confusing. He takes pride in being precise, in helping families and small business owners feel less afraid of the government. The irony of that is not lost on him now.

The event happens three years ago on an evening in late April, during tax season, when he leaves his office after working later than planned. He is tired, carrying his laptop bag and a folder of client documents, and he stops at a convenience store on the way home. Outside, two police officers are questioning a younger man near the entrance. He keeps his eyes down and tries to pass. One of the officers barks at him to stop. He turns, confused, and asks if there is a problem. He says his accent becomes thicker when he is nervous, and he remembers the officer narrowing his eyes as if that alone is suspicious.

What he recalls next comes in flashes, vivid and disconnected. He is told to put his bag down. He asks why. One officer steps closer, pushes him toward the wall, and when he instinctively raises an arm to protect his face, they shout that he is resisting. He remembers the roughness of the concrete against his cheek, a knee in his back, his glasses skidding away. He hears one of them telling him to “calm down” while his body is already pinned and shaking. He tries to explain that he is a tax consultant, that he has papers in the bag, that he is just coming from work. He hears himself speaking too fast in Spanish and English, hears his own voice lose coherence. Someone knees him again. He is handcuffed on the curb while people watch. He says the worst part is not even the pain; it is the sudden knowledge that nothing he says matters.

He is released hours later without charges. The bruises fade over the next weeks, but he says something in him remains “stuck on the sidewalk.” At first he tells almost no one. He misses two days of work and says he had the flu. When he returns to the office, he finds he cannot tolerate hearing sirens from the street below. Each time one passes, his chest tightens and his skin prickles. He starts looking up from his desk to check the window, then checking the lock on his office door, then checking again. Numbers that used to settle him now blur on the page. He rereads the same line of a return five times and still cannot hold it in mind.

Sleep changes quickly. He dreads bedtime because the moment the room goes dark he is back on the pavement, unable to breathe, trying to turn his head while a voice orders him not to move. He wakes soaked in sweat, fists clenched, heart pounding so hard he thinks he might be having a cardiac event. Some nights he walks the apartment until dawn, unable to lie down again. In the morning he is ashamed of how rattled he feels by ordinary things. A client dropping a folder on his desk can make him jump out of his chair.

His world becomes smaller in practical, deliberate ways. He stops going to the convenience store and then to any store after dark. He changes his route home to avoid the block where it happened, even though it adds twenty minutes. He declines invitations from colleagues during tax season, saying he is too busy. Since his divorce, he has lived alone, and now the apartment begins to feel less like freedom and more like a bunker. He keeps the blinds angled shut. If he hears voices in the hallway, he goes silent until they pass.

He notices changes in how he sees other people. Clients who are late or disorganized used to mildly annoy him; now he feels sudden flashes of anger that surprise him. At the same time, he is wary and apologetic, especially with authority figures. If a letter arrives from any government office, even a routine notice, he leaves it unopened for days. He says he used to explain tax law with confidence, but now when clients ask about audits or agencies, he feels a wave of dread, as if he is sending them toward something predatory. He has begun second-guessing his own advice, then staying at the office late to check everything repeatedly.

His adult daughter tells him he seems far away. He wants to be present with her, but during dinner he finds himself scanning the restaurant for uniforms, exits, hands, sudden movements. If a police car drives by, his jaw locks and he loses the thread of conversation. He feels embarrassed by how his body reacts before his mind can intervene. Part of him keeps insisting he should be over it by now; another part believes the world has already shown him exactly what it is.

When he speaks about that night now, he does so in a measured voice, but his hands tremble against his knees. He says he used to think of himself as invisible in a useful way, just another professional man carrying papers home from work. Since the assault, invisibility no longer feels protective. He feels exposed even in routine moments, as if danger can materialize without warning and strip away his dignity in public. He still goes to work, still meets deadlines, still dresses carefully and balances figures to the cent. From the outside, his life appears intact. Inside, much of his energy goes toward staying composed while his body remains braced for the next command, the next shove, the next instant when being harmless will not be enough.
